items.prompt: What is the central idea?
options: Changes in animal coloring gradually force the surrounding landscape to change
The advantage of a color depends on environmental conditions
Individual insects adjust their colors to make their offspring better hidden
Predators cause every member of a population to change color
items.explanation: The passage explains color advantage through background and selection.
items.title: When a dark surface becomes an advantage
items.passage:
Whether an animal’s coloring provides camouflage depends on the background against which it is seen. A dark insect may be difficult to detect on dark bark but conspicuous on a pale surface. A change in the surrounding landscape can therefore change the value of a color without changing how the animal uses it.
Consider a population in which some insects are lighter than others. If birds find insects by sight, the more visible individuals may be caught more often. When darker resting surfaces become common, dark individuals may survive and leave more offspring. Over generations, the proportion of dark insects can increase. This does not mean that individual insects deliberately darken because they need to hide. It means that existing differences affect survival and reproduction under changed conditions.
The relationship is not fixed forever. If the background becomes lighter again, a different color may gain an advantage. Other influences, such as the animals’ resting locations and the presence of predators, can also affect the outcome.
Camouflage thus offers a useful example of selection as a relationship between organisms and their environment. To explain a change in a population, researchers need to examine not only the animals’ appearances, but also the conditions under which those appearances become more or less effective.

items.prompt: Why might replacing old spellings be undesirable?
options: It would make original documents impossible to preserve
It would require every collection to use printed catalogs
It could erase information about historical usage
It would prevent any modern searches from succeeding
items.explanation: The original forms can carry historical and community information.
items.title: Why a catalog preserves old spellings
items.passage:
A reader searching a historical collection may encounter several spellings for the same person or place. It can be tempting to replace every old form with a single modern spelling. Doing so would simplify some searches, but it could also remove information about how names were used in different periods or by different communities.
Catalogers can address this problem by separating the transcription of an original description from the terms used to search it. The original wording remains visible, while an additional reference connects it to other forms of the name. A reader who searches for the modern form can then find older entries without assuming that their spelling has been silently changed.
This approach requires judgment. Similar-looking names may refer to different places, and a name may have changed for political or administrative reasons rather than through spelling variation alone. An automatic rule that merges every resemblance can create false connections. Notes explaining uncertain identifications are therefore valuable, even if they make the catalog appear less tidy.
A useful catalog does more than produce a short list of results. It also helps readers understand how those results were connected. Preserving uncertainty and variation can make a collection more reliable, because the evidence behind a search result remains open to inspection.

items.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why mature forests no longer experience environmental change
The plants that arrive first permanently determine conditions in a forest gap
How changing conditions and prior history shape growth in forest gaps
Increased sunlight is sufficient to explain the order in which plants replace one another
items.explanation: The passage emphasizes a changing sequence and local history.
items.title: How plants respond to a gap in the forest
items.passage:
When a tree falls in a forest, the opening allows more light to reach the ground. Plants that were previously shaded may grow faster, and seeds already present in the soil may begin to develop. Yet a gap is not simply a smaller area with more sunshine. It also changes temperature, moisture, and exposure to wind.
These changes favor different plants at different stages. A species that grows quickly in strong light may occupy open ground before a slower-growing neighbor. As leaves and stems fill the opening, however, conditions begin to change again. Plants able to tolerate shade may persist beneath the developing cover, while those needing intense light may decline.
The outcome depends partly on what was present before the tree fell. Existing seedlings can have an advantage over seeds that arrive later, and the location of nearby adult plants affects which seeds reach the gap. Chance and local history therefore matter alongside broad differences between species.
Forest renewal is best understood as a sequence of changing opportunities rather than a uniform process of replacement. Observing only a freshly opened gap or only a mature patch can miss the transitions that connect them. Following the same opening over time reveals how plants alter the very conditions to which they are responding.

items.prompt: What is the main topic?
options: Why plans are more reliable than observations of a site
How traces in soil can support cautious reconstruction of vanished buildings
How archaeologists determine the exact age of every post
Why wooden buildings leave no evidence after they decay
items.explanation: The talk explains soil traces, patterns and interpretive caution.
items.title: Reading marks left by wooden posts

stimulus.title: Reading marks left by wooden posts
stimulus.script:
A wooden building may disappear long before archaeologists investigate its site. Yet the ground can retain traces of where its supports stood. A hole dug for a post may have been filled with soil different from the surrounding material. After the wood decays, that contrast can remain visible when the surface is carefully exposed.
Individual marks are not always easy to interpret. A dark patch might have resulted from a post, a root, or a later disturbance. The arrangement of several marks can be more informative than one isolated patch. A repeated spacing or a possible line may suggest a structure, especially when it fits other evidence from the site.
But it’s important not to see a complete building too quickly. Once a possible pattern is proposed, there’s a temptation to interpret every nearby mark as part of it. Recording observations before drawing a final outline helps preserve the distinction between what was found and how it is being explained.
Archaeological reconstruction is therefore an argument from several sources of evidence. A plan of a vanished building can be persuasive without being certain in every detail. Showing which parts are well supported and which are tentative makes the reconstruction more useful to later researchers, who may have new evidence or different questions.

items.prompt: What can make a former post location visible?
options: A layer of fresh wood covering the whole excavation
A contrast between its filling soil and the surrounding ground
A root that always grows in the same direction
A permanent label attached by the original builder
items.explanation: Different soil can remain after the wood is gone.

items.prompt: What is the main idea?
options: Borrowed words are adapted through use in a receiving language

items.title: What happens to a borrowed word

stimulus.title: What happens to a borrowed word
stimulus.script:
Languages regularly borrow words from one another. It might seem that borrowing simply transfers a sound and a meaning into a new setting. In practice, a word can change as speakers use it alongside the patterns already familiar in their own language.
Its pronunciation may shift because some sounds are uncommon in the receiving language. Its grammar can change too. A borrowed noun may acquire a local plural ending, for example, even if its source language forms plurals differently. These changes allow speakers to use the word within ordinary sentences rather than treating it as a foreign object each time.
Meaning can also narrow. A source word with several everyday uses may enter another language in connection with a particular food, activity, or object. Later speakers may know only that specialized use. This isn’t necessarily a misunderstanding; it reflects the circumstances in which the word became useful to them.
So a borrowed word is evidence of contact, but it also reveals adaptation. To understand it, we need to consider both where it came from and what speakers did with it afterward. Following only its origin can miss the continuing history of the word in the community that adopted it, including new meanings that develop long after the initial contact.

items.prompt: Why might a borrowed noun receive a new plural ending?
options: It is no longer allowed in ordinary sentences

Its original meaning has been forgotten completely
items.explanation: A local ending integrates the word into the receiving grammar.

items.prompt: Why can stars leave trails in a long exposure from a fixed camera?
options: The camera makes the stars move more quickly
Earth’s rotation changes their apparent positions during the exposure
Each star repeatedly changes its physical size

items.explanation: The fixed camera sees changing sky positions as Earth rotates.
items.title: Recording the night sky

stimulus.title: Recording the night sky
stimulus.script:
A camera aimed at the night sky can produce very different images depending on how long it gathers light. In a short exposure, a star may appear as a small point. During a longer exposure with the camera held still relative to the ground, stars can leave curved trails. The trails reflect the changing direction in which the camera sees them as Earth rotates.
For some purposes, those trails are exactly what the photographer wants. They make a gradual movement visible in a single image. For other purposes, such as examining a faint object in detail, the movement blurs information. Equipment that follows the apparent motion of the sky can help keep an object in the same part of the image while more light is collected.
Neither image is simply more truthful than the other. Each combines a choice of method with a different question. A trail image highlights motion over time, while a tracked image can reveal details that would otherwise be faint or blurred.
This example reminds us that a photograph is not merely a transparent window onto a scene. Exposure time, camera movement, and other decisions shape which features become visible. Understanding those decisions helps us interpret both what an image shows and what it leaves difficult to see.

For other purposes, such as examining a faint object in detail, the movement blurs information. Equipment that follows the apparent motion of the sky can help keep an object in the same part of the image while more light is collected.
Neither image is simply more truthful than the other. Each combines a choice of method with a different question. A trail image highlights motion over time, while a tracked image can reveal details that would otherwise be faint or blurred.
This example reminds us that a photograph is not merely a transparent window onto a scene. Exposure time, camera movement, and other decisions shape which features become visible. Understanding those decisions helps us interpret both what an image shows and what it leaves difficult to see.

items.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
items.question: When evaluating a group project, should a university place more emphasis on the final product or on evidence of the process used to create it? Explain your position and discuss why your preferred approach would lead to fairer or more useful evaluation.
students: The final product should matter most. It shows whether the group achieved its goal, and evaluating the same outcome gives everyone a clear standard. A long record of effort should not outweigh a product that fails to work.

The process deserves more attention. A good result can partly come from luck or from one experienced member. Records of testing and revision reveal what students learned and how they responded when something did not work.
